blocks.robotComment: Same AI, totally different way of talking to it. 🔌
blocks.body: An API (application programming interface) is a defined way for one piece of software to ask another piece of software to do something, and get a result back — without a human clicking any buttons in between. An AI API specifically lets your own code send a request to an AI model and receive its response directly, programmatically.

highlights.text: application programming interface

blocks.body: This is a genuinely different way of using the same underlying AI model compared to a chat app. In a chat app, a human types a message and reads the reply on screen. Through an API, your own program sends the request and decides what to do with the response — show it to a user, save it somewhere, feed it into another step of a larger process, anything code can do.

highlights.text: your own program sends the request and decides what to do with the response

blocks.body: Using an AI model this way usually costs money based on actual usage, billed per request rather than a flat monthly subscription like a consumer chat app might use — worth knowing before building something that could send a very large number of requests.

highlights.text: billed per request

blocks.question: What does using an AI model "via API" actually mean?
options: Your own code sends the request and handles the response directly, instead of a human using a chat app's interface
It means the AI model becomes faster automatically
It's just another name for a chat app's website
It means the AI model requires no cost at all to use
blocks.explanation: An API call is your code talking directly to the model — the human-facing chat interface is a completely separate way of reaching the same kind of underlying model.

blocks.sentence: A defined way for one piece of software to request something from another piece of software is called a(n) ___.
options: API
browser
operating system
blocks.explanation: API stands for application programming interface — exactly this defined request/response mechanism between software.

blocks.statement: Using an AI API is typically billed per request/usage, rather than a single flat subscription price.
blocks.explanation: Usage-based billing is the common model for AI APIs — a real cost consideration once you're building something that sends many requests.

blocks.robotComment: Different providers, same basic recipe underneath. 📦
blocks.body: Nearly every AI API call has the same basic shape, even though the exact details differ between providers: an endpoint (the specific address the request is sent to), an API key (a private credential that proves the request is really from you and lets the provider bill your account), and a payload (the actual content of the request — usually your prompt, plus some settings).

highlights.text: an endpoint
an API key
a payload

blocks.body: The response that comes back is typically structured data (not just plain text) — it usually includes the model's actual answer, plus extra information like how many tokens the request used. Your code reads that structured response and pulls out the specific piece it needs.

highlights.text: structured data

blocks.caption: The exact field names vary by provider, but this request/payload/response shape is consistent across almost all of them.

blocks.body: An API key deserves real caution: it's tied to your account and its usage bill, so it should never be pasted into code that gets shared publicly or shown on screen — treat it the way you'd treat a password, not a piece of ordinary text.

highlights.text: treat it the way you'd treat a password

blocks.question: What is an API key's actual purpose?
options: A private credential that proves a request is really from you and lets the provider bill your account
A public label describing what the request does
A setting that controls the response format
The actual text of your prompt
blocks.explanation: An API key authenticates the request and ties it to your account — it's a credential, not a public label or the prompt itself.

blocks.sentence: The actual content sent in an API request — usually the prompt plus settings — is called the ___.
options: payload
endpoint
response
blocks.explanation: The payload is the actual request content; the endpoint is where it's sent, and the response is what comes back.

blocks.statement: It's safe to paste an API key into code that will be shared publicly, as long as the request itself succeeds.
blocks.explanation: An API key should be treated like a password — exposing it publicly lets anyone use it and run up charges on your account.

lessons.title: Why Build With an API at All

blocks.robotComment: The chat app is great for you. The API is what lets you build something for other people. 🏗️
blocks.body: A chat app is built for one person having a conversation. An API is what you'd reach for the moment you want AI capability embedded inside something else entirely — a feature in an app, a step in an automated workflow, a tool that processes hundreds of documents without anyone typing each request by hand.

highlights.text: embedded inside something else entirely

blocks.body: This matters because it changes what "good AI use" even looks like. A chat app is judged on one conversation going well. A program built on an API is judged on working correctly and predictably across every request it ever sends — including inputs nobody thought to test, and moments when something goes wrong.

highlights.text: working correctly and predictably across every request it ever sends

blocks.body: That's exactly why prompt engineering — deliberately designing prompts for reliability, not just one good result — becomes essential once you're building with an API rather than chatting casually. A prompt embedded in running code can't be quietly reworded by a human mid-conversation if the first attempt goes sideways.

highlights.text: can't be quietly reworded by a human mid-conversation

blocks.question: What is a key difference between using AI through a chat app versus building on top of its API?
options: An API-based program needs to work correctly and predictably across every request, not just one good conversation
The API always produces smarter answers than the chat app
There is no real difference between the two
APIs can only be used by large companies
blocks.explanation: A chat app succeeds if one conversation goes well; a program built on an API needs to hold up across every request it will ever send.

blocks.sentence: Deliberately designing a prompt for reliability, not just one good result, is called ___ — and it becomes essential once a prompt is embedded in running code.
options: prompt engineering
rate limiting
authentication
blocks.explanation: A prompt embedded in code has to work without a human there to reword it mid-conversation — exactly why prompt engineering matters here.

blocks.statement: A program built on an AI API only needs to work well on the specific test inputs its developer happened to try.
blocks.explanation: It needs to hold up across whatever real inputs it actually encounters in use, including ones nobody specifically tested.

options: Working correctly and predictably across every request it sends, not just one good result
How impressive its single best answer ever was
Whether it uses a lot of exclamation points
How quickly one person can type a message

options: prompt engineering
billing

options: Embedding AI capability as a feature inside a larger app or automated workflow

blocks.robotComment: Send a text prompt to an image endpoint and you'll get back... nothing useful. 🚪
blocks.body: You already know an endpoint is the specific address a request is sent to. Most AI providers actually expose several different endpoints, not just one — one built for generating text, another for generating an image, another for turning audio into text, and so on. Picking the right endpoint for the task is the very first decision in assembling a request, before the API key or the payload even come into play.

highlights.text: several different endpoints
Picking the right endpoint for the task is the very first decision

blocks.body: The endpoint you pick isn't just a formality — it determines what shape of payload the request expects and what shape of response comes back. A text-generation endpoint expects a prompt and returns generated text; an image-generation endpoint expects a description and returns image data instead. Sending the wrong shape of payload to the wrong endpoint is a common early mistake.

highlights.text: determines what shape of payload the request expects and what shape of response comes back

blocks.code:
Two conceptual endpoints from the same provider:

endpoint: ".../generate-text"   -> payload expects a text prompt, returns generated text
endpoint: ".../generate-image"  -> payload expects a text description, returns image data

Same provider, same API key — different endpoint, different expected payload shape.
blocks.caption: The endpoint you choose sets the shape of everything that follows in the request.

blocks.question: Why does picking the right endpoint matter before anything else in a request?
options: It determines what shape of payload the request expects and what shape of response comes back
It changes how much the API key costs
It has no real effect on the request
It only matters for image-based tasks
blocks.explanation: The endpoint sets the expected payload shape and response shape — sending a text-generation payload to an image endpoint (or vice versa) won't work.

blocks.sentence: Most AI providers expose more than one endpoint, each built for a different ___.
options: kind of task
password
currency
blocks.explanation: Different endpoints exist for different kinds of tasks — text generation, image generation, and so on — each expecting its own payload shape.

blocks.statement: All endpoints from the same provider expect the exact same payload shape, regardless of what task they perform.
blocks.explanation: Different endpoints are built for different tasks and expect different payload shapes — a text endpoint and an image endpoint won't take the same fields.

blocks.robotComment: The key isn't part of your question — it's proof of who's asking. 🔑
blocks.body: You already know the API key is a private credential that proves a request is really from you. In an actual request, the key isn't buried inside the payload alongside your prompt — it's attached to the request as its own separate piece, alongside the endpoint and the payload, so the provider can check who's asking before it even looks at what's being asked.

highlights.text: attached to the request as its own separate piece

blocks.body: This separation matters: the provider checks the API key first, independent of the payload's contents. An invalid or missing key gets rejected before your prompt is ever read — authentication happens before anything about the actual request is considered.

highlights.text: authentication happens before anything about the actual request is considered

blocks.code:
Conceptual request with the key kept separate:

endpoint:  ".../generate-text"
api_key:   "sk-••••••••••••"   <- checked first, on its own
payload:   {
             prompt: "List three uses for a spreadsheet.",
             max_output_length: 80
           }

If api_key is missing or invalid: request rejected — payload never even gets read.
blocks.caption: The API key is checked independently of whatever the payload contains.

blocks.question: Where does the API key sit in a request, relative to the payload?
options: As its own separate piece, checked independently before the payload's contents are considered
Inside the payload, mixed in with the prompt text
It replaces the endpoint entirely
It's only needed if the payload is very long
blocks.explanation: The API key is a separate piece from the payload — the provider authenticates the key first, independent of what the payload contains.

blocks.sentence: An invalid or missing API key gets a request rejected ___ the payload is ever read.
options: before
after
during
blocks.explanation: Authentication happens first — an invalid key means the payload's contents are never even considered.

blocks.statement: The API key is typically embedded inside the payload, as one of the prompt settings.
blocks.explanation: The API key is kept as its own separate piece of the request, not mixed into the payload.

blocks.robotComment: Same three pieces as Level 1 — just watch them all click together this time. 🧩
blocks.body: Put the last two lessons together with what you already know, and assembling a request is really just answering three questions in order: which endpoint matches the task, what API key authenticates the request, and what payload actually carries the prompt and settings. Every AI API call, no matter the provider, is built from answering those same three questions.

highlights.text: which endpoint matches the task, what API key authenticates the request, and what payload actually carries the prompt and settings

blocks.body: Here's a slightly richer example than Level 1's: imagine building a feature that turns a customer complaint into a one-sentence summary for a support dashboard. The endpoint is the provider's text-generation address. The API key authenticates your account. The payload carries the complaint text and a setting capping how long the summary can be.

highlights.text: turns a customer complaint into a one-sentence summary

blocks.caption: One coherent example: the endpoint decides where it goes, the key decides who it's from, the payload decides what's actually being asked.

blocks.question: When assembling an API request, what three things do you need to decide, in order?
options: Which endpoint matches the task, what API key authenticates it, and what payload carries the prompt and settings
Which programming language to use, how fast the internet is, and the time zone
The color scheme, the font, and the app icon
How many people will read the response
blocks.explanation: Every request comes down to the same three decisions: endpoint, API key, and payload — regardless of provider.

blocks.sentence: In a request, the ___ carries the actual prompt text along with any settings.
options: payload
endpoint
api_key
blocks.explanation: The payload is where the actual prompt and settings live — the endpoint is the address, the key is the credential.

blocks.statement: Assembling an AI API request looks fundamentally different depending on which provider you use.
blocks.explanation: The exact field names vary, but the underlying shape — endpoint, key, payload — is consistent across providers.

options: independently
randomly

questions.statement: The underlying shape of an API request — endpoint, key, payload — stays consistent across different providers, even though exact field names vary.

questions.sentence: In a request, the ___ is where the actual prompt text and settings live.
options: payload
endpoint
api_key

questions.question: Why might sending a text-generation payload to an image-generation endpoint fail?
options: Because each endpoint expects a different payload shape suited to its specific task

blocks.robotComment: The answer is in there somewhere — your code just has to know where to look. 🔍
blocks.body: You already know the response that comes back from an API call is structured data, not just plain text. That means the actual answer isn't the whole response — it's sitting inside one specific field of it, alongside other fields like usage information. Your code has to read that specific field to get anything useful out of the response.

highlights.text: the actual answer isn't the whole response

blocks.body: Think back to Level 1's example response: it had an output field with the actual generated text, plus a tokens_used field for billing info. Grabbing the entire response object and treating it as 'the answer' would mean displaying billing metadata to a user right along with the actual text — clearly not what you want.

highlights.text: Grabbing the entire response object and treating it as 'the answer' would mean displaying billing metadata to a user

blocks.code:
Same response shape as Level 1, viewed as "everything sent back":

response: {
            output: "Photosynthesis converts light into chemical energy.",
            tokens_used: 41,
            finish_reason: "complete"
          }

The answer your code actually wants is just the "output" field — everything else is metadata about the call.
blocks.caption: Only one field here is "the answer" — the rest describes the call itself.

blocks.question: Why can't your code just treat the entire response object as 'the answer'?
options: Because the response is structured data with multiple fields — only one of them holds the actual generated content
Because responses never contain any useful data
Because the endpoint blocks access to the response
Because the API key needs to be included in the answer
blocks.explanation: A response typically bundles the actual output together with metadata like token counts — your code needs to read the specific field that holds the real content.

blocks.sentence: A response often includes both the actual generated content and extra ___ like token counts.
options: metadata
endpoints
passwords
blocks.explanation: Metadata (like token usage) rides alongside the actual answer in the response — it's not part of the answer itself.

blocks.statement: An API response is typically just one long block of plain text with no internal structure.
blocks.explanation: Responses are structured data with multiple named fields — the actual answer is usually just one of them.

blocks.robotComment: Different provider, different field name — same job for your code. 🏷️
blocks.body: The exact name of the field holding the real answer differs between providers — one might call it output, another might call it text or result. Whatever it's called, your code needs to know that specific field name to correctly pull out the actual content, the same way it needs the right endpoint address.

highlights.text: differs between providers

blocks.body: This is why reading a provider's documentation matters before writing anything that depends on the response: guessing the wrong field name means your code either crashes or, worse, silently grabs something that isn't the actual answer.

highlights.text: silently grabs something that isn't the actual answer

blocks.caption: The field name is part of what you learn from a provider's documentation, not something you can assume.

blocks.question: What's the risk of assuming a response field name without checking documentation?
options: Your code might crash or silently grab the wrong piece of data instead of the actual answer
The request will cost more money automatically
The API key will stop working
Nothing — all providers use identical field names
blocks.explanation: Field names vary by provider — assuming the wrong one means your code either fails outright or quietly reads the wrong data.

blocks.sentence: The exact field name holding the real answer in a response ___ between different providers.
options: differs
never changes
is illegal
blocks.explanation: Field names for the actual answer vary by provider, so you need to check documentation rather than assume.

blocks.statement: Every AI provider uses the exact same field name for the response field containing the actual answer.
blocks.explanation: Field names differ between providers even though the underlying idea — one field holds the real answer — stays the same.

lessons.title: When Success Isn't the Whole Story

blocks.robotComment: A request going through isn't a guarantee the answer inside is actually useful. 🚧
blocks.body: A request can succeed — no error, no rejection, the provider accepted it and sent something back — and still not give you what you actually needed. The response might come back with an empty output field, a result that doesn't match what you asked for, or content your code wasn't expecting at all.

highlights.text: succeed
an empty output field, a result that doesn't match what you asked for, or content your code wasn't expecting at all

blocks.body: This is exactly why checking the response before using it matters, even when the request technically worked. Good code validates: is the expected field actually present? Is it empty? Does it look like a reasonable answer, or something clearly off? Skipping that check means bugs show up as bad output shown to a real user, not as an obvious crash.

highlights.text: checking the response before using it matters, even when the request technically worked

blocks.code:
A request that "succeeds" but still needs a second look:

response: {
            output: "",
            tokens_used: 2,
            finish_reason: "complete"
          }

No error was returned — but output is empty. Code that skips checking this would show nothing (or crash) instead of catching the problem.
blocks.caption: Technically successful and still not usable — this is exactly what a validation check is for.

blocks.question: Why does a successful request still need its response checked before use?
options: Because a request can succeed technically while still returning an empty or unexpected result
Because successful requests always cost more
Because checking the response cancels the API key
Because it's not possible for a request to fail
blocks.explanation: Success just means the provider accepted and processed the request — it doesn't guarantee the result inside is actually usable.

blocks.sentence: Good code checks a response's content — is the field present, is it empty, does it look reasonable — ___ using it.
options: before
after
never
blocks.explanation: Validating a response before using it catches empty or unexpected results before they reach a user.

blocks.statement: If an API request succeeds with no error, the content it returns is guaranteed to be exactly what your code expected.
blocks.explanation: A request can succeed while still returning an empty or unexpected result — success and usefulness aren't the same thing.

questions.question: Why is treating the entire response object as "the answer" a mistake?
options: Because the response is structured data — only one specific field holds the actual generated content
Because responses are always encrypted
Because the endpoint hides the real answer permanently
Because the API key must be included in every field

questions.statement: An API response typically bundles the actual answer together with other metadata, like token usage.

questions.sentence: The response field name that holds the actual answer ___ between different providers.
options: differs
is identical
is illegal

questions.question: What should you check before relying on a response field name in your code?
options: The provider's documentation, since field names vary between providers
Nothing — all providers use the same field names
The device battery level
The color of the response text

questions.statement: A request can technically succeed and still return an empty or unexpected result.

questions.sentence: Good code checks a response for problems ___ using its content.
options: before
after
never

questions.question: What does it mean when an API request "succeeds" but the expected field is empty?
options: The provider accepted and processed the request, but the actual content still needs validating before use
The API key was rejected
The endpoint does not exist
The request was never actually sent

questions.statement: Skipping response validation means problems are more likely to show up as bad output shown to a real user, rather than an obvious crash.

questions.sentence: A response bundling the real answer together with details like token counts is an example of ___ data.
options: structured
unstructured
encrypted

questions.question: Which of these is a genuine reason to validate a response before using it?
options: A request can succeed while still returning an empty, missing, or unexpected result
